title: Cloud Strategy in Government Context
objectives: Navigate Cloud First policy and understand what it actually requires
Evaluate cloud options through the G-Cloud framework and procurement realities
Assess and manage vendor lock-in risks in government cloud deployments
Apply NCSC cloud security guidance to architecture decisions
Develop pragmatic strategies for cost management and exit planning
whyThisMatters:
Cloud is no longer a technology choice in UK government. It is policy. The Cloud First mandate means that any new service must demonstrate why cloud is not suitable before choosing an alternative. But policy and reality are different things. Most government departments operate in a hybrid world where some workloads run in public cloud, some sit in Crown Hosting, and some remain stubbornly on-premises in data centres that were supposed to close five years ago. The architect's job is to navigate between the policy aspiration and the operational reality.

This matters because cloud decisions are among the most consequential an architect makes. They determine your cost profile for years. They shape your supplier relationships. They constrain your future options. They define your security boundary. Getting cloud strategy wrong does not just mean technical problems. It means budget overruns that embarrass your department, vendor dependencies that limit your negotiating power, and security configurations that keep the NCSC awake at night.

The challenge is that cloud strategy in government is not the same as cloud strategy in the private sector. Government has unique constraints around data sovereignty, procurement rules, security classification, and political sensitivity. A strategy that works brilliantly for a startup or a bank may be entirely inappropriate for a department handling OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE citizen data under public scrutiny. This lesson equips you to make cloud decisions that are technically sound, commercially sensible, and politically survivable.

content.heading: Cloud First Policy: What It Actually Means
content.body:
The UK Government Cloud First policy, introduced in 2013, states that when procuring new or existing services, public sector organisations should consider and fully evaluate potential cloud solutions first before considering any other option. This sounds straightforward. In practice, it is widely misunderstood.

Cloud First does not mean Cloud Only. It does not mean every workload must run in public cloud. It does not mean you cannot use on-premises infrastructure. It means cloud should be your default starting position, and if you choose something else, you should be able to explain why. The policy creates a presumption in favour of cloud, not a prohibition against alternatives.

What Cloud First actually requires in practice: when you are designing a new service or replacing an existing one, you should evaluate public cloud options genuinely and fairly. If cloud is suitable, use it. If it is not suitable for legitimate reasons (security classification, latency requirements, cost at scale, regulatory constraints), document why and choose the appropriate alternative. The key word is 'evaluate.' You must actually consider cloud, not dismiss it reflexively because your department has always used on-premises infrastructure.

The policy also connects to the broader Technology Code of Practice, which emphasises using commodity services, avoiding lock-in, and making things open. Cloud services, particularly platform and software services, align well with these principles because they are shared, standardised, and maintained by specialists.

However, there is a gap between policy intent and departmental reality. Many departments adopted cloud in name but not in practice. They lifted and shifted virtual machines into cloud infrastructure without redesigning for cloud-native patterns, gaining the costs of cloud without the benefits. Others adopted cloud enthusiastically but without proper cost governance, discovering that pay-as-you-go pricing can be significantly more expensive than on-premises when workloads are predictable and constant.

The architect's role is to apply Cloud First intelligently: genuinely evaluating cloud options, choosing cloud where it delivers real benefit, choosing alternatives where cloud is genuinely inappropriate, and being honest about the trade-offs in either direction. Dogmatic cloud adoption is as harmful as dogmatic cloud avoidance.

content.heading: The G-Cloud Framework and Procurement Realities
content.body:
G-Cloud is the UK government's procurement framework for cloud services. It operates through the Digital Marketplace, where suppliers list their cloud hosting, cloud software, and cloud support services. Government buyers can search the marketplace, compare services, and call off contracts without running a full procurement exercise for each purchase. In theory, this makes buying cloud services fast and simple. In practice, it is more complicated.

The G-Cloud framework is genuinely useful for straightforward cloud purchases. If you need a standard AWS or Azure subscription, a SaaS tool for project management, or a cloud hosting provider for a simple web application, G-Cloud lets you procure it in days rather than months. The framework agreements are pre-negotiated, the terms are standardised, and the process is well understood by procurement teams.

Where G-Cloud becomes complicated is at scale or for complex requirements. The framework has spending thresholds and contract length limits. Large cloud commitments (the kind where you negotiate enterprise agreements with reserved instances and committed spend discounts) do not fit neatly into G-Cloud's transactional model. Departments spending millions per year on a single cloud provider often need to negotiate separately, which means longer procurement timelines and more commercial complexity.

The Digital Marketplace also lists hundreds of suppliers, which creates a paradox of choice. For commodity services like basic hosting, the choice is overwhelming and the differentiation is minimal. For specialist services, the right supplier may not be on the framework at all, requiring alternative procurement routes.

Practical implications for architects: understand your department's procurement rules and timelines before making architecture decisions that depend on specific cloud services. A technically optimal architecture that requires a supplier not on G-Cloud, or a contract structure that does not fit the framework, will face procurement delays that can derail your delivery timeline. Work with your commercial team early. They are not obstacles. They are navigators of a complex system that exists for good reasons around public accountability and fair competition.

Also understand that G-Cloud pricing is list pricing. Large departments with significant cloud spend should be negotiating enterprise agreements that offer substantial discounts. If your department is paying list price for millions of pounds of cloud services, that is a commercial failure, not a technical one, but architects should be aware of it when estimating costs.

content.heading: Choosing Between AWS, Azure, and GCP in Government
content.body:
All three major cloud providers operate UK regions and hold the necessary security certifications for government workloads up to OFFICIAL (including OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE). The choice between them is not primarily a technical decision. It is a commercial, strategic, and ecosystem decision.

AWS has the longest history in UK government and the largest market share. Many departments started their cloud journey on AWS, and it has the broadest service catalogue. The Government Digital Service (GDS) runs significant infrastructure on AWS. If your department already has AWS expertise, established accounts, and negotiated pricing, there is a strong pragmatic argument for staying there unless you have specific reasons to move.

Microsoft Azure has grown significantly in government, particularly in departments with heavy Microsoft licensing (which is most of them). The integration between Azure and Microsoft 365, Active Directory, and the broader Microsoft ecosystem makes it attractive for departments whose identity, collaboration, and productivity tools are already Microsoft. Azure's hybrid story (Azure Arc, Azure Stack) is also strong for departments managing the transition from on-premises.

Google Cloud Platform has a smaller government footprint in the UK but offers strong capabilities in data analytics, machine learning, and Kubernetes-native workloads. Some departments choose GCP for specific analytical workloads while running their primary infrastructure elsewhere.

The honest reality is that for most government workloads, all three providers offer equivalent core capabilities. The differentiators are: existing skills and expertise in your team, existing commercial agreements and pricing, integration with your current tooling and identity systems, specific service capabilities that one provider offers and others do not, and your department's risk appetite for concentration with a single supplier.

What architects should avoid is choosing a cloud provider based on personal preference or familiarity. The decision should be documented, justified against your specific requirements, and made with commercial and security input. It should also acknowledge that this is a long-term commitment. Switching cloud providers mid-programme is expensive and disruptive. Choose deliberately and for defensible reasons.

Some departments are making explicit multi-cloud decisions, using different providers for different workloads based on best fit. This is legitimate but adds operational complexity. We will discuss this trade-off in the multi-cloud section.

content.heading: Vendor Lock-in: Understanding and Managing It
content.body:
Vendor lock-in is the most frequently cited concern in government cloud strategy discussions. It is also the most frequently misunderstood. Lock-in is not binary. It exists on a spectrum, and some degree of lock-in is inevitable and acceptable. The question is not 'how do we avoid all lock-in?' but 'what level of lock-in is acceptable given our requirements, and how do we maintain enough optionality to exit if we need to?'

Lock-in occurs at multiple levels. Infrastructure lock-in (using provider-specific virtual machine types, storage services, or networking configurations) is relatively shallow. You can migrate VMs between providers with effort but without redesigning your application. Platform lock-in (using provider-specific managed services like AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, or Google Cloud Run) is deeper. Your application code depends on the provider's APIs and runtime environment. Data lock-in (storing large volumes of data in provider-specific formats or databases with high egress costs) is often the deepest and most expensive to escape.

The pragmatic approach to lock-in in government involves several principles. First, distinguish between commodity services and differentiating services. For commodity capabilities (compute, storage, basic networking), use provider services but keep your configuration portable through infrastructure-as-code tools like Terraform that abstract provider specifics. For differentiating capabilities (the things that make your service work), make a deliberate decision about whether the provider's managed service is worth the lock-in versus building on more portable foundations.

Second, always have an exit strategy, even if you never use it. This means understanding what it would cost and how long it would take to move your workloads to an alternative provider. You do not need to build for portability from day one, but you need to know what portability would require. This information is essential for commercial negotiations because a supplier who knows you cannot leave has no incentive to offer competitive pricing.

Third, protect your data. Data portability is more important than application portability. Applications can be rewritten. Data cannot be recreated. Ensure you can export your data in standard formats, that you understand egress costs, and that your data architecture does not depend on proprietary features that have no equivalent elsewhere.

Fourth, use open standards and open-source technologies where they meet your needs. Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, and standard APIs are portable across providers. Provider-specific equivalents may offer convenience but increase switching costs. This is a trade-off, not a rule. Sometimes the managed service is worth the lock-in because it reduces operational burden significantly.

content.heading: Multi-Cloud vs Single-Cloud Strategies
content.body:
The multi-cloud debate in government often generates more heat than light. Advocates argue it prevents lock-in and enables best-of-breed selection. Critics argue it doubles operational complexity without delivering proportionate benefit. Both are partially right.

Genuine multi-cloud (running the same workload across multiple providers for resilience or portability) is expensive and complex. It requires abstracting away provider-specific features, maintaining expertise across multiple platforms, managing multiple commercial relationships, and operating multiple security configurations. Very few government programmes have the scale, budget, or team capability to do this well. For most departments, genuine multi-cloud is an aspiration that sounds good in strategy documents but proves impractical in delivery.

What most departments actually practice is multi-cloud by accident or by portfolio. Different programmes chose different providers at different times, and the department now has workloads spread across AWS, Azure, and perhaps GCP. This is not a strategy. It is a consequence of decentralised decision-making. It creates operational overhead (multiple skill sets, multiple security configurations, multiple commercial agreements) without the strategic benefits of deliberate multi-cloud.

The pragmatic middle ground for most government departments is a primary cloud provider strategy with exceptions. Choose one provider as your default for most workloads. Invest in skills, tooling, and commercial agreements for that provider. Allow exceptions where a specific workload has requirements that the primary provider cannot meet well, but treat exceptions as exceptions that require justification.

This approach gives you most of the benefits of standardisation (skills concentration, commercial leverage, operational simplicity) while preserving the option to use alternatives where genuinely needed. It also maintains some market leverage because the supplier knows you could move workloads if the relationship deteriorates.

The key architectural decision is where to draw the abstraction boundary. If you abstract everything to be provider-agnostic, you lose the benefits of managed services and increase development cost. If you use provider-specific services everywhere, you maximise lock-in. The sensible approach is to use provider-specific services for operational concerns (monitoring, logging, identity) where switching cost is manageable, and to be more cautious about lock-in for core business logic and data storage where switching cost is high.

content.heading: Data Sovereignty and UK Regions
content.body:
Data sovereignty is a critical concern for government cloud deployments. UK government data, particularly citizen data, must be stored and processed in appropriate jurisdictions. This is not just a preference. It is a legal and policy requirement that constrains your cloud architecture decisions.

All three major cloud providers now operate UK regions (AWS has London and a planned second region, Azure has multiple UK regions, GCP has a London region). For most OFFICIAL workloads, UK regions provide adequate data sovereignty. Your data stays in the UK, processed on infrastructure in the UK, subject to UK law.

However, data sovereignty is more nuanced than just where the data physically sits. Consider: where does the cloud provider's support staff access your data from? Where are backups replicated? Where does metadata about your usage flow? Where are the management plane APIs hosted? A service running in a UK region may still have control plane dependencies on US or European infrastructure. For most OFFICIAL workloads, this is acceptable. For OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE workloads with specific handling requirements, you need to understand these data flows in detail.

For SECRET and above, public cloud is generally not appropriate without specific arrangements (such as AWS's dedicated government regions or specialised sovereign cloud offerings). Most Solution Architects in civilian departments will not encounter these classifications, but you should know the boundary exists.

Practical implications for architects: always specify UK regions explicitly in your infrastructure configuration. Do not rely on defaults, which may route to the nearest region (which could be Ireland or continental Europe). Understand your data classification and the handling requirements that flow from it. Work with your security team to confirm that your chosen cloud services meet the data residency requirements for your specific data types. Document your data sovereignty approach explicitly in your architecture documentation because assessors will ask about it.

Also be aware that data sovereignty requirements may change. Brexit created uncertainty about data adequacy with the EU. Future regulatory changes could impose new requirements. Design your architecture so that data location is a configurable parameter rather than a hardcoded assumption.

content.heading: Cloud Security in Government: NCSC Guidance
content.body:
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) provides specific guidance for government organisations using cloud services. This guidance is practical, well-written, and should be your primary reference for cloud security decisions. It is not optional. Departments are expected to follow NCSC guidance, and security assessors will check that you have.

The NCSC Cloud Security Principles define 14 areas that you should evaluate when choosing and configuring cloud services. These cover data in transit protection, asset protection and resilience, separation between customers, governance framework, operational security, personnel security, secure development, supply chain security, secure user management, identity and authentication, external interface protection, secure service administration, audit information, and safe and secure use of the service.

In practice, the major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) meet most of these principles at the platform level. Your responsibility as an architect is to ensure that your use of the platform also meets them. The provider secures the cloud. You secure what you put in the cloud. This shared responsibility model is fundamental and frequently misunderstood.

Common security mistakes in government cloud deployments: overly permissive IAM policies because 'we will tighten them later' (you will not). Public S3 buckets or storage accounts because someone needed quick access during development. Unencrypted data at rest because encryption was not configured by default. Logging disabled or not monitored because nobody set up the alerting. Security groups or network ACLs that allow broad access because the original developer could not work out the minimum required permissions.

The architect's security responsibilities in cloud: define the security architecture before deployment, not after. Specify encryption requirements (at rest and in transit). Define the identity and access management model. Specify network segmentation and access controls. Define logging and monitoring requirements. Ensure the security configuration is codified in infrastructure-as-code so it cannot drift. Work with your security team to conduct a cloud-specific threat assessment.

NCSC also provides guidance on specific patterns like zero trust architecture in cloud environments, secure configuration of specific services, and incident response in cloud contexts. Reference these in your architecture documentation to demonstrate that your security approach is grounded in authoritative guidance rather than personal opinion.

content.heading: Cost Management and FinOps Basics
content.body:
Cloud cost management is where many government departments have been caught out. The promise of cloud is that you pay only for what you use. The reality is that without active cost governance, cloud spending grows unpredictably and often exceeds what the equivalent on-premises infrastructure would have cost. This is not a failure of cloud. It is a failure of cost management.

The fundamental challenge is that cloud makes it easy to provision resources and hard to track what you are spending. A developer can spin up a large database instance for testing and forget to shut it down. A team can over-provision their production environment 'just in case' and never right-size it. Data transfer costs accumulate invisibly. Reserved instance commitments expire and workloads revert to expensive on-demand pricing. Without active management, costs drift upward continuously.

FinOps (Financial Operations) is the practice of bringing financial accountability to cloud spending. It involves three capabilities: informing (understanding what you are spending and why), optimising (reducing waste and improving efficiency), and operating (making cost-aware decisions as part of normal delivery).

Practical cost management for government architects:

First, establish cost visibility from day one. Tag all resources with project, team, and environment identifiers. Set up cost dashboards that show spending by service, by team, and by environment. Make cost information visible to the teams that generate it, not just to finance.

Second, right-size your resources. Most government cloud deployments are over-provisioned. Production environments sized for peak load that occurs once a year run at 10% utilisation the rest of the time. Use auto-scaling where possible. Review instance sizes quarterly. Shut down non-production environments outside working hours.

Third, use commitment discounts appropriately. Reserved instances and savings plans offer 30-60% discounts for committed usage. For stable, predictable workloads (and government has many of these), committed pricing is almost always cheaper than on-demand. But commit only to what you are confident you will use. Unused reservations are wasted money.

Fourth, design for cost efficiency. Architecture decisions have cost implications. Serverless architectures are cheap at low volume but expensive at high volume. Managed databases cost more than self-managed but require less operational staff. Data transfer between regions or out of the cloud is surprisingly expensive. Consider cost as a non-functional requirement during design, not as a surprise during operation.

Fifth, budget and forecast. Cloud spending should be budgeted like any other cost. Set spending alerts at 80% and 100% of budget. Review forecasts monthly. Treat unexpected cost increases as incidents that require investigation, not as inevitable consequences of cloud adoption.

content.heading: The Hybrid Reality and Exit Strategies
content.body:
Despite Cloud First policy, most government departments operate in a hybrid world. They have workloads in public cloud, workloads in Crown Hosting or co-location facilities, and workloads on-premises in departmental data centres. This is not a failure of strategy. It is a reflection of reality. Legacy systems that cannot be easily migrated, regulatory requirements that constrain data location, commercial contracts that have years left to run, and applications that genuinely perform better on dedicated infrastructure all contribute to a hybrid landscape.

The architect's job is not to pretend this hybrid reality does not exist. It is to design coherent architectures that work across it. This means addressing connectivity between environments (typically VPN or dedicated connections like AWS Direct Connect or Azure ExpressRoute), consistent identity and access management across environments, and careful security design at the boundary between cloud and on-premises. The network boundary between environments is a trust boundary that requires explicit security controls.

Teams operating services that span cloud and on-premises need consistent tooling for deployment, monitoring, and incident response. Running completely different operational models for different parts of the same service creates cognitive overhead and increases the risk of operational failures.

Crown Hosting deserves specific mention. It provides government-grade data centre facilities for workloads that cannot or should not run in public cloud. It is not cloud, but it is not traditional on-premises either. It offers better physical security, resilience, and connectivity than most departmental data centres. For workloads that need dedicated infrastructure but not the full flexibility of public cloud, Crown Hosting is a legitimate and well-supported option.

Exit strategies are essential even if you never use them. An exit strategy means understanding what it would cost and how long it would take to move your workloads away from your current provider. This is not about planning to leave. It is about maintaining negotiating leverage and managing risk. A department that cannot exit its cloud provider is commercially captive. The provider knows this and prices accordingly.

Practical exit strategy elements: maintain infrastructure-as-code that could be adapted for an alternative provider. Keep data in standard, exportable formats. Understand your egress costs (the charges for moving data out of a cloud provider, which can be substantial at scale). Document the dependencies on provider-specific services and estimate the effort to replace them. Review and update this assessment annually. Share it with your commercial team so they can use it in contract negotiations.

The pragmatic approach is to accept hybrid as a transitional state and design for it explicitly. Document which workloads are where and why. Define clear integration patterns for cross-environment communication. Plan migration paths for workloads that should move to cloud but have not yet. Accept that some workloads may never move, and design your architecture to accommodate them gracefully rather than treating them as embarrassing exceptions.

workedExample.title: HMRC Cloud Migration Strategy for Tax Platform
workedExample.context: HMRC operates one of the largest technology estates in UK government, processing over 40 million tax returns annually. Their existing tax platform runs primarily on-premises in departmental data centres with some workloads in Crown Hosting. The platform comprises approximately 300 applications, ranging from modern microservices to COBOL-based mainframe systems. The department has committed to a Cloud First approach for new services and a phased migration of existing workloads, but needs a coherent strategy that addresses the full complexity of their estate. The annual technology spend is approximately 700 million, of which infrastructure accounts for roughly 180 million.
workedExample.approach:
The architecture team develops a cloud strategy based on workload classification rather than a blanket migration approach.

They classify workloads into four categories. Category 1 (Cloud Native): new services and recently built microservices that can run natively on cloud platform services. These move to AWS (HMRC's primary cloud provider) using managed services, containers, and serverless where appropriate. Category 2 (Cloud Ready): applications that can run in cloud infrastructure with minimal modification. These are lifted and shifted to cloud VMs as an interim step, then progressively modernised. Category 3 (Cloud Constrained): applications with specific requirements (latency, data classification, regulatory) that limit cloud options. These move to Crown Hosting or remain on-premises with explicit justification. Category 4 (Legacy Bound): mainframe and legacy applications where migration cost exceeds replacement cost. These remain in place with a separate modernisation or replacement roadmap.

For vendor strategy, they choose AWS as the primary provider based on existing skills, established commercial agreements, and the scale of their existing AWS footprint. Azure is permitted for specific workloads that integrate heavily with Microsoft tooling. GCP is not used to avoid spreading skills too thinly.

For cost management, they establish a FinOps team that provides cost visibility, manages reserved instance purchases, and works with delivery teams to optimise spending. They negotiate an enterprise agreement with AWS that provides significant discounts on committed spend.

For security, they implement a cloud security baseline aligned with NCSC guidance, enforced through infrastructure-as-code templates that teams must use. All cloud deployments go through a security review gate that checks compliance with the baseline.

For exit strategy, they document the cost and effort required to migrate their top 20 workloads to an alternative provider. This information is used in commercial negotiations and updated annually.
workedExample.outcome: Over three years, HMRC migrates 60% of eligible workloads to AWS, reduces data centre footprint by 40%, and achieves a 15% reduction in infrastructure unit costs. The FinOps team identifies and eliminates 12 million per year in cloud waste (unused resources, over-provisioned instances, unoptimised data transfer). The security baseline prevents three potential data exposure incidents that would have occurred under the previous ad-hoc security approach. The exit strategy documentation strengthens their negotiating position in the AWS enterprise agreement renewal, securing improved pricing terms.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The key insight was that cloud migration is not a single decision but hundreds of individual decisions, each requiring assessment against specific criteria. The workload classification framework gave teams a clear decision model rather than expecting every team to develop their own cloud strategy. The FinOps investment paid for itself within six months through waste elimination. The exit strategy, though never used, proved its value as a commercial negotiation tool. The biggest challenge was cultural: convincing teams that Cloud First did not mean migrating everything immediately, and that keeping some workloads on-premises was a legitimate, defensible decision.

civilServiceScenario.title: Ministry of Justice Cloud Strategy After Supplier Exit
civilServiceScenario.background: The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has been running its digital services primarily on a managed hosting contract with a single supplier. The contract expires in 18 months and the supplier has indicated they will not bid for renewal at current pricing. The MoJ's digital estate includes: the prison population management system (critical, handles sensitive data), the legal aid application service (public-facing, moderate traffic), internal case management systems (200+ users, complex integrations), and several smaller services. The current annual hosting cost is 14 million. The department has limited cloud skills internally, having relied on the managed service provider for infrastructure operations.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must develop a cloud strategy that migrates the department's services to a sustainable hosting model within 18 months, while maintaining service continuity, managing security requirements for sensitive criminal justice data, building internal cloud capability, and staying within budget constraints. The department cannot afford a gap in service when the current contract expires.
constraints: 18-month deadline before current hosting contract expires
Limited internal cloud skills and experience
Sensitive criminal justice data with strict handling requirements
Budget for migration must come from existing technology allocation
Must maintain service continuity throughout migration
Some systems are poorly documented with limited vendor knowledge transfer
Political sensitivity around criminal justice system availability
Must comply with Cloud First policy and NCSC security guidance
Need to demonstrate value for money to Treasury
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Chief Solution Architect responsible for developing and presenting the cloud migration strategy. You must balance technical ambition with delivery realism, manage the security implications of moving sensitive data to cloud, and build a strategy that the department can actually execute with its current capability.
civilServiceScenario.discussion: This scenario forces you to confront the gap between cloud strategy theory and migration reality. You cannot simply choose a cloud provider and migrate everything. You need to assess each workload, understand its constraints, plan a migration sequence that manages risk, and build the skills to operate in cloud while still running the existing estate. Consider: which workloads move first (the easy ones to build confidence, or the critical ones to reduce contract dependency)? How do you handle the prison population system, which cannot tolerate downtime and handles highly sensitive data? How do you build cloud skills in a team that has never operated cloud infrastructure? What is your fallback if migration takes longer than 18 months? How do you manage the commercial transition from a single managed service to potentially multiple cloud services requiring internal operational capability?

practiceArtefact.description: For the Ministry of Justice scenario above, produce a cloud strategy decision paper that covers: (1) Your recommended cloud provider and justification, (2) A workload classification and migration priority for the four main systems, (3) Your approach to security for sensitive criminal justice data in cloud, (4) A high-level timeline showing migration sequence, (5) Your exit strategy and lock-in mitigation approach.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Be realistic about what can be achieved in 18 months with limited cloud skills. Consider the risk profile of each workload and sequence migrations accordingly. Address the security concerns head-on rather than glossing over them. Think about what happens if things take longer than planned. Consider the commercial and skills implications alongside the technical ones. Your paper should be suitable for a departmental technology board, so write for a mixed audience of technical and non-technical readers.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
CLOUD STRATEGY DECISION PAPER: Ministry of Justice Hosting Transition

Recommendation: Adopt AWS as primary cloud provider, migrate workloads in risk-managed phases over 18 months, retain Crown Hosting for the prison population system during initial transition, and invest in internal cloud operations capability.

Cloud Provider Selection: AWS recommended based on: broadest government track record and existing NCSC-assessed security posture, strongest ecosystem of government-experienced support partners (needed given limited internal skills), most mature tooling for migration from traditional hosting, and availability through G-Cloud for rapid procurement. Azure considered but rejected as primary due to weaker migration tooling for non-Microsoft workloads and less government-specific operational guidance.

Workload Classification and Migration Priority:

Phase 1 (Months 1-6): Legal aid application service. Rationale: public-facing, moderate complexity, well-documented, lower security sensitivity than criminal justice systems. This builds team confidence and cloud operational capability with manageable risk. Target: cloud-native deployment on AWS using containers and managed services.

Phase 2 (Months 4-10): Internal case management systems. Rationale: internal users provide a more forgiving environment for migration issues. Complex integrations require careful planning but data sensitivity is lower than prison systems. Target: lift and shift to AWS with progressive modernisation.

Phase 3 (Months 8-14): Smaller services. Rationale: individually low risk, can be migrated in parallel once team has established cloud operational patterns. Target: cloud-native where practical, lift and shift where time-constrained.

Phase 4 (Months 12-18): Prison population management system. Rationale: highest risk, highest sensitivity, requires proven cloud operational capability before migration. Target: initial migration to Crown Hosting as interim step, with full cloud migration planned for months 18-24 (beyond current contract deadline, requiring short-term Crown Hosting arrangement).

Security Approach: All criminal justice data classified as OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE with specific handling requirements. AWS UK regions used exclusively. Encryption at rest and in transit mandatory. Dedicated VPC with no internet-facing components for criminal justice workloads. NCSC Cloud Security Principles assessment completed for each workload before migration. Security baseline enforced through infrastructure-as-code templates. Penetration testing before each phase goes live.

Timeline Risk: The prison population system is unlikely to migrate fully to cloud within 18 months given its complexity and sensitivity. Recommend negotiating a 6-month Crown Hosting arrangement as a bridge. This is an honest assessment of delivery risk rather than an optimistic plan that will fail.

Exit Strategy: Architecture designed using Terraform for infrastructure-as-code (provider-portable). Data stored in standard formats (PostgreSQL, S3-compatible storage). Application code uses standard APIs rather than AWS-specific SDKs where practical. Annual assessment of migration cost to Azure as alternative. Exit cost estimated at 2.1 million and 9 months for the full estate.

Skills Investment: Recruit two senior cloud engineers immediately. Enrol existing team in AWS certification programme. Engage AWS Professional Services for Phase 1 with explicit knowledge transfer requirements. Target: self-sufficient cloud operations capability by month 12.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about your department's current cloud usage. Is it a deliberate strategy or an accumulation of individual decisions? What would a coherent strategy look like, and what would need to change to get there?

Consider a workload you are responsible for that runs on-premises. If you had to justify why it is not in cloud (as Cloud First policy requires), could you? Is the justification genuinely technical, or is it inertia?

How well does your department understand its cloud costs? Could you tell someone what you spent on cloud last month, broken down by service and team? If not, what does that tell you about your cost governance?

Think about your exit strategy for your primary cloud provider. If they doubled their prices tomorrow, how long would it take you to move? What would it cost? If you do not know, what does that mean for your commercial negotiating position?

Consider the security of your cloud deployments. Are your IAM policies as restrictive as they should be? Is all data encrypted? Are you monitoring for security events? Be honest about the gaps between your security architecture documentation and your actual configuration.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the UK Government Cloud First policy actually require?
options: All government services must run in public cloud
Cloud solutions must be evaluated first, with alternatives requiring justification
Departments must use AWS as their primary cloud provider
On-premises infrastructure is no longer permitted for new services
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cloud First creates a presumption in favour of cloud, requiring organisations to evaluate cloud options genuinely before considering alternatives. It does not mandate cloud for all workloads. If cloud is not suitable for legitimate reasons, alternatives are acceptable provided the decision is documented and justified.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective approach to managing vendor lock-in in government cloud deployments?
options: Avoid all provider-specific services and build everything on open-source alternatives
Use multiple cloud providers for every workload to maintain portability
Accept some lock-in deliberately, maintain an exit strategy, and protect data portability
Choose the cheapest provider and switch whenever a better deal appears
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Complete lock-in avoidance is impractical and expensive, sacrificing the benefits of managed services. The pragmatic approach is to accept lock-in where the benefits justify it, maintain a documented exit strategy for commercial leverage, and prioritise data portability because data cannot be recreated while applications can be rewritten.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the shared responsibility model for cloud security, what is the customer's primary responsibility?
options: Physical security of the data centres
Patching the hypervisor and host operating system
Securing their own data, applications, identity management, and network configuration
Ensuring the cloud provider meets NCSC Cloud Security Principles
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The shared responsibility model means the cloud provider secures the infrastructure (the cloud itself), while the customer secures what they put in the cloud: their data, applications, IAM policies, network configuration, and encryption settings. Many security failures in government cloud deployments result from misunderstanding this boundary.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most pragmatic cloud strategy for most government departments?
options: Genuine multi-cloud with every workload running across multiple providers
A primary cloud provider with justified exceptions for specific workloads
Avoiding cloud entirely and using Crown Hosting for all workloads
Splitting workloads equally across AWS, Azure, and GCP for maximum leverage
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A primary provider strategy with exceptions gives most departments the benefits of standardisation (concentrated skills, commercial leverage, operational simplicity) while preserving the option to use alternatives where genuinely needed. Genuine multi-cloud is too complex and expensive for most government organisations to execute well.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most important first step in cloud cost management?
options: Negotiating the largest possible discount with your cloud provider
Moving all workloads to serverless to minimise costs
Establishing cost visibility through tagging, dashboards, and team-level reporting
Setting a hard spending cap that cannot be exceeded
knowledgeCheck.explanation: You cannot manage what you cannot see. Cost visibility through consistent resource tagging, spending dashboards, and team-level reporting is the foundation of cloud cost management. Without visibility, you cannot identify waste, attribute costs to teams, or make informed decisions about optimisation. Discounts and architecture changes come after you understand your current spending.
